pages.title: Backups to a second drive
pages.description: A daily backup of the whole vault to another drive or folder, plain or encrypted with age, kept 7 days, 4 weeks and 6 months, and a restore you can check.
pages.md:
Version history protects you from your own edits, but it lives on the same
disk as the vault. **Backups** copy the whole vault somewhere else, once a
day while Lumen is open.

## Set it up

⌘K → *Backups…*, then choose one of:

- **Back up to a folder or drive…** writes a plain `.tar` archive that any
  archive tool opens.
- **Back up encrypted to a folder or drive…** writes `.tar.age`, encrypted
  with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to a backup key made for you. The
  panel shows the key (`AGE-SECRET-KEY-1…`) once. Keep it away from this
  device: without it nobody can open the backup, you included. Only its
  public half is stored.

A folder that is the vault, or inside it, is refused: backups there would
sync, and every backup would contain the ones before it. Git internals and
the trash aren't backed up.

## What's kept

The newest backup of each of the last **7 days**, **4 weeks** and **6
months**: at most 17 archives. Older ones are deleted after each backup.

## When something's wrong

- A backup that fails (an unplugged drive, a folder the browser no longer
  lets Lumen write to) is shown at once: a notice, and a red line in the
  panel. Lumen tries again after 15 minutes.
- **Three days** without a successful backup is shown once a day.

## Restore

- **Restore everything to a new folder…** puts the newest backup's files
  into a folder you pick.
- **Restore it into the vault** restores one file or folder. Nothing is
  overwritten: a file that's already there is restored next to it, as
  `name (restored 2026-11-10).md`.

Every archive starts with a list of its files and their SHA-256. A restore
checks each file and refuses a damaged archive.

Without Lumen:

```sh
tar -xf lumen-backup-2026-11-10T03-12-00Z.tar
age -d -i backup-key.txt lumen-backup-….tar.age | tar -x
```

## How it's checked

`src/__tests__/backup.test.ts` backs up 1,000 notes and 200 attachments,
deletes the vault and restores it, plain and encrypted: **every file has the
same SHA-256**. It also checks that a broken drive is reported within a
minute, and that a backup writes nothing into the vault.
`e2e/backup-drill.spec.ts` runs the same drill from the panel in the browser.

## Limits

- The browser needs the File System Access API to write to a folder
  (Chromium). The desktop app's own folder access (Tauri) and WebDAV targets
  are behind the same `BackupTarget` interface and come with their pull
  requests.
- Backups run while Lumen is open, so a laptop that's always closed gets
  none. The three-day notice says so.

pages.title: Writing a book
pages.description: Chapters as notes in order, word goals per chapter and per book, today's words and a streak, and the book assembled into a Hebrew EPUB 3 and a print-ready PDF.
pages.md:
A book in Lumen is a folder of notes, one per chapter, and an **index
note** that lists the chapters in order. The index uses the format of
Obsidian's [Longform](https://github.com/kevboh/longform) plugin, so the
same book opens in Obsidian too.

## Start a book

Open any note in the folder and run **Book: chapters, goals and export**
from the command palette (`⌘K` / `Ctrl+K`). When the note is not in a book
yet, Lumen offers to make one: it asks for the title and writes an index
note whose chapters are the folder's notes, in name order (`01`, `02`, …
sort as numbers). **Book: add this note as a chapter** adds the open note to
the end of the book whose index is in the same folder.

The index note looks like this:

```yaml
---
longform:
  format: scenes
  title: The Orchard
  sceneFolder: /
  scenes:
    - Opening
    - - A scene inside the opening   # a nested list: parts of a chapter
    - The second chapter
word-goal: 80000   # the book's goal
daily-goal: 500    # words a day, for the streak
author: Noa Cohen
lang: he
---
```

A chapter's own goal is `word-goal:` in the chapter's frontmatter.
Lumen's keys sit outside `longform:`, which Longform rewrites.

## The book panel

The panel lists the chapters in order with their word counts and goals,
the book's total against its goal, the words written today and the
streak (days in a row on which the daily goal was met). Drag a chapter,
or use its ↑ ↓ buttons, to reorder; only the `scenes:` list in the index
changes. A nested part moves with its chapter. Click a chapter to open it.

Today's words are the book's total now minus its total at the end of the
last day you wrote, so deleting counts against the day. The totals are
kept in a small hidden file next to the index
(`.<index name>.lumen-book.json`, which Obsidian does not show).

### How words are counted

Only prose counts: frontmatter, code, comments (`%% … %%`), link targets,
embeds and Markdown marks do not. A Hebrew word with its prefixes is one
word, also when a hyphen or maqaf joins the prefix to a number or a Latin
word (`ה-CNN`, `ב־1948`); abbreviations with geresh or gershayim (`צה״ל`,
`מס׳`) and maqaf compounds (`בית־ספר`) are one word each. A spaced dash is
not a word.

## EPUB

**Export EPUB** writes `<title>.epub`: a title page, a table of contents,
one file per chapter, the book's font (Frank Ruhl Libre, SIL Open Font
Licence) and the images the chapters show. A Hebrew book opens from the
right in Apple Books, Kindle and other readers
(`page-progression-direction="rtl"`, `dir="rtl"` and `lang="he"` on every
page); an English chapter inside it reads left to right. Links to other
notes become plain text (they lead nowhere in a book); links to the web
stay. The book keeps the same identifier across exports, so a reader keeps
your place and highlights.

## Print and PDF

**Print / PDF** opens the book in a print window; choose **Save as PDF**
in the print dialog. Pages are A5 with the chapter title on a new page,
page numbers at the bottom (none on the title and contents pages), the
paragraph indent of a printed book and Hebrew right to left.

## How it was checked

- `src/__tests__/bookMode.test.ts`: the word count rules, the index (read,
  reorder, add, comments and CRLF kept), progress, the streak, and a
  30-chapter book counted in well under 10 seconds.
- `src/__tests__/bookEpub.test.ts`: the package structure (stored
  `mimetype` first, RTL spine, navigation, font, images), well-formed XHTML
  chapters, 30 chapters assembled in well under 10 seconds, and the print
  document.
- A 30-chapter Hebrew book with footnotes, a table, code and an English
  chapter, assembled in a browser (0.3 s): **epubcheck 5.3.0 — 0 errors,
  0 warnings**; its PDF has 62 A5 pages with Frank Ruhl Libre embedded.

Not yet checked by hand: opening the EPUB in Apple Books and Kindle
Previewer.

pages.title: Calendar sync (CalDAV and ICS)
pages.description: Keep the vault's dated tasks in sync with a CalDAV calendar (Fastmail, Nextcloud, iCloud), and see subscribed calendars' events in the daily note.
pages.md:
:::note[Status]
The sync engine and the daily-note block are in place and tested. The
Settings screen for connecting an account and the conflict dialog come in
the next release, together with native requests in the desktop app.
:::

## Tasks, both ways

Tasks with a date (`📅` due or `⏳` scheduled) sync with one CalDAV task
calendar as VTODOs. An edit on either side reaches the other: create, edit
the text or the date, mark done, delete. Tasks made on the server (on an
iPhone, in Thunderbird, in Nextcloud) are added to the inbox note,
`Tasks/Calendar.md` by default.

Each synced task carries a hidden id at the end of its line:

```markdown
- [ ] Send the report 📅 2026-11-20 <!-- lumen-caldav:lumen-7f3a -->
```

Other Markdown readers don't show it. Don't remove it: without it the task is
new to the calendar.

### When both sides changed

Each sync compares both sides with what they agreed on last time. If only one
side changed, its version wins. If both changed the same task, or one side
deleted a task the other edited, Lumen shows both versions and you choose
(in the conflict dialog):
keep this device's, keep the server's, or keep both. Nothing is overwritten
without asking.

## Subscriptions in the daily note

Add a calendar's ICS address (a "secret address" or a `webcal://` link) and
that day's events appear in each daily note, in a block between
`<!-- lumen-calendar:start -->` and `<!-- lumen-calendar:end -->`. The block
is read-only and is replaced on refresh. The rest of the note is never
touched. Recurring events, multi-day events and moved instances are handled.

## Privacy

- The password and the subscription addresses are kept only in the secret
  store, never in settings, files or logs. A private ICS address is itself a
  key.
- Every request appears in the privacy ledger as "CalDAV task sync" or
  "Calendar subscription".

## Desktop and web

In the web app, the server must allow this app's origin (CORS). If it
doesn't, Lumen says so instead of failing silently. The desktop app will send the
requests itself, so CORS won't apply there.

## Tested

200 random changes on both sides against a local Radicale server, with
conflicts answered at random, lost 0 tasks and duplicated 0. Create, done and
delete each reached the other side in one sync, in under half a second.

pages.title: Note cards and image export
pages.description: Put vault notes on the canvas as live cards, edit them in place, and export the canvas as PNG, SVG or PDF with Hebrew intact.
pages.md:
## Note cards

A note card is a note from your vault placed on the canvas. It shows the
note's title and first lines, and it moves, resizes, groups, sits in frames
and takes arrows like any other shape.

- **Add a card**: in the canvas bar, **+ Note card**, then type a note's
  name or `![[note]]`. You can also paste one or more `![[note]]` lines
  onto the canvas; each one becomes a card.
- **Edit in place**: click the card, click it again to work inside it, then
  double-click its text. `⌘Enter` (or clicking outside) saves into the
  note, and `Esc` cancels. The frontmatter is kept as it was.
- **Open**: the card's **Open** button closes the canvas and opens the note
  in a tab.

Names resolve the way Obsidian resolves them. A full path wins; otherwise
the note with that file name and the shortest path is used. A card whose
note was moved or deleted says so.

In the `.excalidraw` file a card is an embed whose link is
`lumen-note:<path>`. In [JSON Canvas](/workspace/json-canvas/) it's a
`file` node, as in Obsidian Canvas. Importing a `.canvas` turns its
Markdown file nodes into cards; images and other files stay as shapes.

Only the cards in view are drawn, and each note is read once, so a canvas
with 50 cards opens in under 1.5 seconds.

## Export: PNG, SVG, PDF

Use **PNG**, **SVG** and **PDF** in the canvas bar.

- Note cards are drawn as their title and first lines. Hebrew cards are
  aligned right.
- **SVG** fixes how Excalidraw writes right-to-left text. Each line gets
  its own direction and is placed on the side where the canvas draws it.
  Without this, right-aligned Hebrew would fall outside the image.
- SVG also embeds the Hebrew font (Assistant, limited to the Hebrew range),
  so the file looks the same on a computer without Hebrew fonts.
- **PNG** is drawn at twice the size, after the Hebrew font has loaded.
- **PDF** prints the SVG on a page of its own size. Choose "Save as PDF",
  and the Hebrew stays text you can select.

Everything is exported on this device. The fonts come from the app itself.

pages.title: Diagrams on the canvas (Mermaid and "draw me")
pages.description: Turn Mermaid into shapes you can edit on the canvas, or describe a diagram and let a model on this device draw it.
pages.md:
**Diagram…** in the canvas bar opens the diagram dialog. The diagram is
placed in the middle of the view as ordinary canvas shapes: boxes,
arrows and labels you can move, restyle and connect to the rest of the
canvas.

## From Mermaid

Paste a Mermaid definition and choose **Insert** (or press `⌘Enter`).
Five types become editable shapes:

| Type | First line |
|---|---|
| Flowchart | `flowchart TD`, `flowchart LR`, `graph TD` |
| Sequence | `sequenceDiagram` |
| Class | `classDiagram` |
| State | `stateDiagram-v2` |
| Entity–relationship | `erDiagram` |

Other Mermaid types (mindmap, gantt, pie, …) are inserted as a picture of
the diagram, and the dialog says so first.

Before converting, the definition is checked with Mermaid itself, and a
syntax error is shown with Mermaid's message. After converting, every
label of the definition is looked for in the new shapes. If any is
missing, the dialog stays open and names them.

Hebrew labels work in every type. In an ER diagram, entity names must be
Latin: put the Hebrew in the entity's alias, as in
`CUSTOMER["לקוח"] { string name }`.

## "Draw me"

Describe the diagram in a sentence (in Hebrew or English) and choose
**Draw**. A model on this device writes the Mermaid, which then appears in
the dialog for you to check before inserting.

- It runs **only on a local model**: Ollama on this computer, or the model
  in the browser (Settings → AI). It never uses the cloud chat, whatever
  the AI policy says, so nothing leaves the device.
- The answer has to be one of the five editable types and pass Mermaid's
  check. If it doesn't, the model gets the error back and tries again,
  up to twice.
- The labels stay in the language of your request.

The target is a valid diagram for at least 80% of 20 test requests on a
local 7B model. It is measured with
`npm run eval:canvas-draw -- --model qwen2.5:7b`.

pages.title: Canvas (Excalidraw)
pages.description: The whiteboard — on Excalidraw, saved as open .excalidraw files in your vault, fully on your device — and what happens to your old tldraw canvases.
pages.md:
The canvas (`🎨 Canvas / Whiteboard`, `⌘K`) is
[Excalidraw](https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw): shapes, arrows,
free-hand drawing, text, images and frames, with Excalidraw's own tools,
menus and keyboard shortcuts, in the language of the interface. Excalidraw is
MIT licensed and runs fully on your device. (Until October 2026 the canvas was
tldraw, which needs a licence key in production and contacts its CDN.)

## Nothing leaves the device

Under the **local-only** policy the canvas makes zero network requests, and
under every policy it makes none that carry your drawing:

- Excalidraw's fonts are served by Lumen itself, from `/excalidraw/fonts/`,
  not from a CDN, and are cached for offline use the first time they load.
- Its interface translations are part of the app.
- Excalidraw's AI, collaboration, "shareable link" and library-browser
  features are switched off.

Every canvas is saved automatically, half a second after a change, to
`canvases/<name>.excalidraw` in your vault. The last change is written when
you close the canvas or switch to another one.

## Hebrew and right-to-left text

Type Hebrew into a text element and it is laid out right-to-left while you
edit it. Excalidraw's hand-drawn fonts have no Hebrew glyphs, so Lumen draws
Hebrew letters with **Assistant** (the Hebrew font Excalidraw ships) inside
every canvas font — mixed Hebrew/English text keeps both. With the interface
in Hebrew or Arabic, Excalidraw's menus and panels are right-to-left too.

## Your old tldraw canvases

## Where canvases live

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| `canvases/<name>.tldr` (tldraw snapshot) | `canvases/<name>.excalidraw` (Excalidraw scene, open JSON) |

An `.excalidraw` file is the standard Excalidraw format. It opens in any
Excalidraw app, and it is pretty-printed, so diffs stay readable in a
git-synced vault.

## Converting

Command: `🎨 Canvas: convert tldraw canvases to Excalidraw`. The canvas
picker also lists each `.tldr` (and each `.canvas.json` from the first Lumen
whiteboard) that has no `.excalidraw` yet, with a **Convert** button.

It converts every `.tldr` canvas in the vault in one go and reports how many
were converted, skipped or failed, plus a warning list per canvas. It runs
on your device and makes no network requests.

**The backup.** Your `.tldr` files are never changed, renamed or deleted.
Each one stays next to its new `.excalidraw` file. If a canvas already has an
`.excalidraw` file, it is skipped, so your Excalidraw work is never
overwritten. Running the command twice does nothing the second time.

## What converts

| tldraw | Excalidraw |
|---|---|
| Rectangle, ellipse, diamond (with label) | Rectangle, ellipse, diamond, with the label bound inside |
| Triangle, trapezoid, rhombus, pentagon, hexagon, octagon, star, block arrows | A closed polygon, with the label grouped with it |
| Cloud, heart, oval | Ellipse |
| Check box, x box | Rectangle (the inner mark is dropped) |
| Text | Text: same characters, size and colour |
| Sticky note | Filled rectangle with the text inside |
| Arrow, including its label and bend | Arrow, curved through the same midpoint, label bound to it |
| Arrow connected to a shape | Arrow bound to the same shape, at both ends |
| Frame and the shapes in it | Frame, with its shapes inside |
| Group | Excalidraw group (nested groups too) |
| Image embedded in the canvas | Image, with crop and flip |
| Freehand drawing, highlighter | Freehand stroke (pen pressure kept) |
| Line | Line (smooth if it was a spline) |

Ids, positions, sizes, rotation, opacity, locks, links and colours carry
over. Colours map to the closest Excalidraw colour, and sizes to stroke widths
and font sizes.

## What doesn't convert exactly

Every one of these is kept as something you can see and is listed in the
warning report. Nothing is dropped silently.

- **A frame inside a frame.** Excalidraw frames don't nest. The inner frame
  becomes a top-level frame, and its shapes stay in it.
- **Elbow arrows** become straight arrows.
- **Video, embeds, bookmarks and unknown shapes** become a dashed rectangle
  labelled with the shape type, and the link is kept on it.
- **Images that weren't embedded** (a web address or a missing file) become
  a placeholder with the link. Nothing is downloaded during the conversion.
- **More than one page.** Excalidraw has a single scene, so later pages are
  placed to the right of the previous one.
- **Text formatting** (bold, italic, links inside text) becomes plain text.
  List bullets and numbers are kept as characters.

## Hebrew and right-to-left text

Text is copied exactly, character for character. Excalidraw text has no
direction setting, so the conversion sets the alignment: text that tldraw
aligned to the *start* is aligned right when it begins with Hebrew or Arabic,
and left otherwise.

Converted Hebrew text is drawn with Assistant, like text typed in the canvas.

## Older canvases

The converter reads every format a canvas may have been saved in: what the
current tldraw canvas saves, older tldraw snapshots (plain text instead of
rich text, arrows connected the old way), and `.tldr` files exported from
tldraw itself. Canvases from the first Lumen whiteboard (`.canvas.json`) convert
straight to Excalidraw from the canvas picker: each card becomes a note at
its position (its connections never had an equivalent).

pages.title: WhatsApp and Telegram chats into notes
pages.description: Import an exported WhatsApp or Telegram chat into notes, one per day or one per chat, with its media, entirely on this device.
pages.md:
Decisions, recipes and study material often live in a chat. **⌘K → Import
a WhatsApp or Telegram chat…** turns an exported chat into notes. The files
are read on this device and nothing is sent anywhere.

## Export the chat

| App | How | What to pick in Lumen |
|---|---|---|
| WhatsApp (Android) | Chat → ⋮ → More → **Export chat** → with or without media → save to Files | The `.txt` (and the media files), or the `.zip` |
| WhatsApp (iPhone) | Chat → contact or group name → **Export Chat** → Save to Files | The `.zip` (it holds `_chat.txt` and the media) |
| Telegram Desktop | Chat → ⋮ → **Export chat history** → format **JSON** | `result.json`, plus the `photos/` and `files/` folders, or all of it zipped |

You can pick several files at once: the chat and its media, or more than one
chat.

## What you get

Each chat becomes a folder in `Imported/`, for example
`Imported/Family (WhatsApp)/`, with:

- **one note per day** (`2026-11-12.md`), or **one note for the whole chat**
  with a heading per day. You choose when you import.
- frontmatter: the app, the chat, the date, the participants and the number
  of messages.
- every message in order, with its time and author. System lines (someone
  joined, encryption notices) are in italics.
- media copied into `media/` next to the notes: pictures shown in place,
  other files linked. A file the export left out is named in the note, so
  nothing disappears silently.
- WhatsApp's `*bold*`, `_italic_` and `~strike~` become Markdown, and
  Telegram's bold, links and code blocks are kept.

Nothing existing is overwritten: a second import of the same chat goes into
a new folder (`… 2`). The folder is marked as outside content, so AI agents
treat its text as other people's words.

## Dates in every language

The export is written in the phone's language, and Lumen reads both Hebrew
and English exports:

- Hebrew: `12.11.2026, 14:03 - טל: …` and 12-hour times with לפנה״צ / אחה״צ.
- English: US `11/12/26, 2:03 PM - …` and day-first `12/11/2026, 14:03`.
- Arabic, with Arabic-Indic digits and ص / م. The digits are read as numbers
  only in the date and time: a message keeps the digits it was written with.
- iPhone's `[12.11.2026, 14:03:12]` form, and the invisible direction marks
  iPhones add around names and attachments.
- An export without media: Android's `` / `<המדיה לא נכללה>`,
  and the iPhone's line per kind, in English and in Hebrew (`image omitted` /
  `התמונה הושמטה`, `video omitted` / `סרטון הווידאו הושמט`, voice, GIF,
  sticker, document and contact card). A document keeps its file name.

WhatsApp doesn't write the date order anywhere, so Lumen works it out from the
whole file: a number over 12 must be the day. Otherwise, if the dates only run
forward when read one way, that way is right. When every date could still be
read either way, dots mean day first, slashes with an English AM/PM mean the
US order, and slashes with an Arabic or Hebrew clock (ص / م, לפנה״צ / אחה״צ)
mean day first. Otherwise the day comes first, as in Israel and Europe.

## One message into the inbox

A single message shared or pasted into **Quick capture** keeps where it came
from. WhatsApp's copied form `[14:03, 12.11.2026] Tal: …` and Telegram
Desktop's `Tal, [12.11.2026 14:03]` become an inbox entry that starts with
`WhatsApp · Tal · 2026-11-12 14:03`. On Android, the share sheet sends the
message to the installed app (see [Quick capture](/workspace/quick-capture/)).
Plain text is captured as before.

pages.title: Database formulas and map view
pages.description: Computed columns for the database block — syntax, every function, limits — and the map view for notes with coordinates.
pages.md:
A `database` block can add **formula columns**: values computed from each
note's frontmatter. They show up in every view, and the filter, sort and
group controls can use them like any other property.

```database
source: shop/
type: item
formulas:
  total: price * qty
  big: total >= 100          # a formula can use the ones above it
  late: if(due < today() and status != "done", "late", "")
  שנה: year(תאריך)
```

Every formula column is shown: with `fields:` in the spec, the formula
columns not listed there come after the listed fields (list one in
`fields:` to put it elsewhere). Formula cells are read-only (they are not written to the notes). A note a
formula can't compute — say `price: "n/a"` in `price * qty` — shows
**error** in that cell, with the reason on hover; the other notes are
unaffected.

## Trying a formula

Click **ƒ Formula column** above the view, give the column a name and type
a formula: it is checked as you type, and **Add column** shows it at once.
To keep it, copy the line it shows into the block's `formulas:`.

**Write with AI** turns a description ("days left until the due date, and
nothing once it's done") into a formula, using the local model (Ollama or
in-browser). The answer is checked by the same parser: a formula that does
not parse, calls an unknown function or uses a property the database does
not have is sent back to the model with the error, so what you get always
parses.

## Syntax

| | |
|---|---|
| Numbers | `12`, `3.5`, `.5`, `1e3` |
| Text | `"text"` or `'text'`; `\"` and `\\` inside |
| Yes / no / nothing | `true`, `false`, `null` |
| Lists | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| Properties | `price`, `תאריך`, `meta.owner`; `prop("due date")` for names with spaces or symbols |
| The note itself | `file.name`, `file.path`, `file.folder` |
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %`, `^` (power, right to left: `2 ^ 3 ^ 2` is 512) |
| Text join | `&`, or `+` when a side is plain text |
| Comparison | `=` (`==`), `!=` (`<>`), `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` — not chained (`a < b < c` is an error) |
| Logic | `and` / `&&`, `or` / `||`, `not` / `!` |

Precedence, loosest first: `or`, `and`, `not`, comparison, `&`, `+ -`,
`* / %`, unary `-`, `^`. Keywords and function names are case-insensitive.

**Values** follow the filter's rules: numbers stay numbers, numeric text
(`"12"`) counts as a number, `YYYY-MM-DD` text compares as a date, a list
equals a value it holds (`tags = "fav"`), `=` compares text ignoring case,
and `<` / `>` order text by character code — the same result in every
language setting (alphabetical for Hebrew; capitals before small letters).
An empty property makes arithmetic empty (`price * qty` with no `qty` is
empty, not an error). `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.3`.

**Dates** are in UTC, so a formula gives the same answer in every time
zone: `2026-10-20` is midnight UTC, and a time written without an offset
(`2026-10-20T12:00`) is read as UTC too. `date + 7` and `date - 7` move by days; `date - date` is the number
of days between them.

## Functions

**Logic**

- `if(condition, then, else?)` — `then` when the condition holds, else `else` (empty when left out). Only the branch taken is computed.
- `and(a, b, …)`, `or(a, b, …)`, `not(x)`
- `coalesce(a, b, …)` (or `ifempty`) — the first argument that is not empty
- `empty(x)` — no value, empty text or empty list
- `prop("name")` — the property called name

**Text**

- `concat(a, b, …)` — joined as text
- `len(x)` (or `length`) — characters in text (Hebrew letters count one each), items in a list
- `upper(text)`, `lower(text)`, `trim(text)`
- `contains(textOrList, value)` — ignoring case; for a list, whether it holds the value
- `startswith(text, prefix)`, `endswith(text, suffix)` — ignoring case
- `replace(text, find, with)` — every occurrence; plain text, not a pattern
- `slice(text, start, end?)` (or `substring`) — 0-based; negative counts from the end
- `left(text, n)`, `right(text, n)`, `repeat(text, n)`
- `join(list, separator?)` — `", "` unless given; `split(text, separator)` — a list
- `text(x)` — as text (dates as `YYYY-MM-DD`); `number(x)` — as a number, empty when it is not one

**Math**

- `abs(x)`, `floor(x)`, `ceil(x)`, `sqrt(x)`, `pow(x, y)`, `mod(x, y)`
- `round(x, digits?)` — halves away from zero; `round(1.005, 2)` is `1.01`
- `min(…)`, `max(…)`, `sum(…)`, `avg(…)` (or `average`), `count(…)` — numbers or lists of numbers; empty values are skipped

**Dates**

- `today()`, `now()`
- `date("2026-10-20")`, `date(2026, 10, 20)`
- `year(d)`, `month(d)` (1–12), `day(d)`, `weekday(d)` (1 = Sunday … 7 = Saturday)
- `dateadd(d, n, unit?)` — unit `"days"` (default), `"weeks"`, `"months"`, `"years"`, `"hours"`, `"minutes"`; Jan 31 + 1 month is Feb 28
- `datediff(later, earlier, unit?)` — whole units from earlier to later (a month counts once its day is reached)

## Errors and limits

Every problem is reported as a formula error with the character it is at:
a syntax error, an unknown function, the wrong number of arguments, a value
of the wrong type (`"a" * 2`), or math that has no answer (division by
zero, `sqrt(-1)`, a number too large).

Formulas run in Lumen's own interpreter over a fixed set of operations and
the functions above — never as JavaScript, so a formula cannot reach
anything but the note's frontmatter. Each one has fixed limits, counted in
steps rather than time, so it always finishes and the same formula always
behaves the same way:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Length of a formula | 2,000 characters |
| Nesting (parentheses, calls, chained operators) | 64 levels |
| Parts in a formula | 1,000 |
| Steps for one note | 20,000 |
| Length of a text value | 20,000 characters |
| Items in a list value | 2,000 |

Plugin-defined formula functions (running in a QuickJS sandbox) are
planned; they will add to this list without changing the built-ins.

## Map view

The **Map** tab places every note that has coordinates on a map
(OpenStreetMap tiles; Leaflet is loaded only when you open the tab). A
note's coordinates come from:

- the property named by `location:` in the spec, or else
- a `location` (or `coordinates`) property, or else
- `lat` (or `latitude`) and `lng` (or `lon`, `longitude`) properties.

A location can be written `"32.08, 34.78"`, `[32.08, 34.78]` or
`{lat: 32.08, lng: 34.78}`. Click a marker for the note's title (which opens
it) and a few of its fields. Notes without coordinates are counted under
the map.

```database
source: trips/
view: map
location: place
fields: [date, rating]
```

pages.title: Database views
pages.description: Editable Table / Cards / Kanban / List / Calendar views over your YAML frontmatter.
pages.md:
The `database` block turns any folder of markdown notes (with consistent
YAML frontmatter) into a queryable collection — and renders the result
as one of five interactive views — and lets you edit it.

## Tag your notes

Drop YAML frontmatter on every note you want to include:

```yaml
---
type: book
title: Invisible Cities
author: Italo Calvino
rating: 5
status: reading
cover: https://example.com/cover.jpg
---

(body…)
```

The fields you use are entirely up to you — `type` is the only one Lumen
treats specially (it's the row filter).

## Drop a database block

```database
source: books/         # folder under workspace root
type: book             # filter by frontmatter.type
view: kanban           # table | cards | kanban | list | calendar | map
where: status != "done" AND (rating >= 4 OR contains(tags, "fav"))
groupBy: status        # kanban columns; sections in the other views
columns: [want, reading, done]   # kanban columns shown even when empty
sort: [-rating, title] # '-' (or ' desc') for descending
fields: [title, author, rating, status]
cover: cover           # for cards
```

Lumen scans the workspace, matches every note where `frontmatter.type`
equals `book` and the `where:` filter holds, and renders the requested view.
(`sortBy:` and `view: gallery` from older specs still work.)

## Filter

`where:` — and the **Filter** box above the view — take an expression over
the frontmatter, after Dataview's `WHERE`:

- `AND` / `&&`, `OR` / `||`, `NOT` / `!`, parentheses. `AND` binds tighter.
- `=` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=`. Numbers compare as numbers, `YYYY-MM-DD`
  dates as dates. `tags = "fav"` is true when the list holds `fav`.
- `contains(field, "x")`, `startswith(…)`, `endswith(…)`, `empty(field)`.
- `file.name`, `file.path`, `file.folder` describe the note itself.
- Field names may be in any script: `סטטוס = "הושלם"`.

The **Sort** and **Group** menus re-order and section the view without
changing the spec.

## Views

- **Table** — click a cell (or focus it and press F2) to edit it; Enter
  saves, Escape cancels; checkboxes toggle. Long tables render only the
  rows on screen. Click a title to open the note.
- **Cards** — cover image + key fields. Set `cover: <fieldName>` to pick
  which frontmatter URL becomes the card image.
- **Kanban** — columns by `groupBy`. Drag a card by its handle to another
  column to change that property — or with the keyboard: focus the handle,
  Space, ← / →, Space (Escape cancels).
- **List** — titles with a few fields.
- **Calendar** — agenda of every note with a parseable `dateField`.
- **Map** — a marker per note with coordinates (`location: "32.08, 34.78"`,
  or `lat` + `lng`). See [Database formulas and map view](/workspace/database-formulas/).

## Formula columns

`formulas:` adds computed columns — `total: price * qty`,
`late: if(due < today(), "late", "")` — that the filter, sort and group can
use too. Syntax and every function: [Database formulas and map
view](/workspace/database-formulas/).

## Editing

An edit changes that one value in that one note's frontmatter — comments,
quoting, key order and the note's body stay exactly as they were. A note
whose frontmatter doesn't parse is never written (you get a message
instead). Editing the note that is open goes through its editor, so undo
works.

## Live updates

Edit a note in another tab and the database view re-runs the query
automatically (a `lumen-workspace-changed` event triggers the refresh).

## Tips

- Mix views — keep one big database block at the top of a hub note and
  switch between Kanban and Gallery with the tab strip.
- Combine with **Smart Insert** — drop a YAML spec on an empty line and
  Lumen wraps it as a `database` fence for you.
- Values that are maps or nested lists show as read-only text; edit them in
  the note.

pages.description: Find broken links, orphans and near-duplicate notes across the workspace, without AI.
pages.md: Command: `🩺 Vault Doctor: Check Workspace` (`⌘K`). Vault Doctor reads every Markdown note in the open workspace folder and opens a report in a new tab. The report links to every note it mentions, so you can click straight through to fix things. It runs entirely on your device and makes no AI calls. | Check | What it finds | |---|---| | Broken wiki links | `[[Note]]` where there is no such note and no such heading in the same note. When exactly one note name is close (same words, or at most two typos), the report suggests it. | | Missing headings | `[[Note#Heading]]` or `[[#Heading]]` where the heading doesn't exist. | | Broken Markdown links | Relative links to `.md` files that don't exist. `../` and `%20` are resolved. | | Ambiguous names | Two notes with the same file name. `[[name]]` can only open one of them. | | Near-duplicates | Notes whose text overlaps by about 80% or more (MinHash over 5-word shingles). | | Images without alt text | `![](…)` and `` with no `alt`. | | Empty notes | Nothing besides front matter. | | Orphans | Notes that no other note links to. `index`, `README`, `home` and `welcome` don't count as orphans. | Links inside code blocks and inline code are ignored. ## Applying the suggested fixes Command: `🩺 Vault Doctor: Apply Suggested Link Fixes`. This rewrites every broken wiki link that has a single suggestion, for example `[[Projct Plan]]` → `[[Project Plan]]`. Labels and `#heading` parts are kept. You get a list of the changes to confirm first. Notes that are open in a tab are skipped, so unsaved edits are never overwritten. ## Known limitations — status | Id | Limitation | Status | |---|---|---| | A1 | A code fence indented past a list item's content column | Fixed. Indented 4 or more spaces past the column, it is indented code inside the item (as CommonMark reads it), so links in it and after it at that indentation are ignored. | | A2 | An HTML block of type 7 after a line that is all inline code | Fixed. That line is paragraph text, so a lone tag on the next line is inline HTML and the links after it are checked. | | A3 | `&` inside a double-backtick code span in a heading | Fixed. Character references stay literal in code spans of any backtick length, as in the rendered heading id. |

pages.title: Embedded queries and saved searches
pages.description: A ```query block lists the notes that match a search, a ```dataview block runs common Obsidian Dataview queries, and saved searches sit in the sidebar. All of them update as the vault changes.
pages.md:
## ```query blocks

Write a search in a `query` block and the preview lists the notes that
match it, kept up to date as you save notes:

````markdown
```query
tag:project -tag:done
view: table
sort: modified desc
limit: 20
```
````

The search uses the same [operators](/workspace/search-operators/) as the
search dialog: words, `tag:`, `path:`, `"exact phrase"`, `/regex/` and
`-term` to leave notes out. Lines of the form `option: value` set how it
shows:

| Option | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `view` | `list`, `table` (note, folder, modified, tags) | `list` |
| `sort` | `relevance`, `name`, `path`, `modified` — then `asc` or `desc` | `relevance` |
| `limit` | 1–500 | 50 |

A line starting with `//` is a comment. The note that holds the block is
never in its own results. An option it can't read is shown above the
results, not silently dropped.

## ```dataview blocks

Vaults that come from Obsidian are full of
[Dataview](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/) blocks.
Lumen runs the common part of its query language, so they render here
without the plugin:

````markdown
```dataview
TABLE status, due FROM #project WHERE status != "done" SORT due ASC
```
````

- **`LIST [expr]`** and **`TABLE [WITHOUT ID] expr [AS "name"], …`**
- **`FROM`** `#tag`, `"folder"`, `[[note]]` (notes that link to it), with
  `AND`, `OR`, `-` and parentheses
- **`WHERE`** comparisons (`= != < > <= >=`), `and` / `or` / `!`, `+ - * /`
- **`SORT`** one or more fields, `ASC` / `DESC`; **`LIMIT`** n
- Fields: front matter, inline fields (`key:: value`, `[key:: value]`) and
  `file.name`, `file.path`, `file.folder`, `file.link`, `file.mtime`,
  `file.ctime`, `file.size`, `file.tags`, `file.outlinks`
- Functions: `contains`, `icontains`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `length`,
  `lower`, `upper`, `date(today)`, `dur(7 days)`, `default`, `choice`,
  `round`, `number`, `string`, `join`, `regexmatch`

`TASK`, `CALENDAR`, `GROUP BY`, `FLATTEN` and DataviewJS are not supported:
the block says so instead of guessing. Nothing in a query is run as code —
the language is parsed and interpreted, and a test checks that the query
code has no `eval`.

## Live updates

Both kinds of block re-run when a note is saved, deleted or renamed. In a
vault of 1,000 notes, re-running after a save takes well under 100 ms.

## Saved searches

In the search dialog, **☆ Save search** keeps the search. Saved searches are
listed at the top of the file sidebar; a click opens the dialog on that
search again, and × removes it. They are kept in this browser, not in the
vault.

pages.title: EPUB reader and reading mode
pages.description: Read EPUB books in the vault (Hebrew right-to-left included), highlight them like PDFs, and read clipped pages in a calm reading mode.
pages.md:
Lumen opens EPUB books from your vault in a reader of its own. Your books,
their fonts and pictures stay on the device: nothing is fetched while you
read. A link in a book that leads to a website is shown, not opened.

## Open a book

- **Command palette** (⌘K / Ctrl+K) → **Open an EPUB for reading…** copies a
  book from your computer into the vault and opens it.
- **File tree**: click a `.epub` file.
- **A link** in a note: `[[book.epub]]`, or `[[book.epub#chapter=3]]` to open
  it at chapter 3.

book's table of contents. The arrow keys go to the previous or next chapter;

are shown right to left, with the book's own fonts.

**Light**, **Sepia** or **Dark**, **A−** / **A+** for the text size, and
**⇥⇤** / **⇤⇥** for the line width. The settings are kept for each book (and
each note in reading mode) on this device.

Select text and press **Highlight** (or **H**). Highlights work like the

highlight, or remove it, under **Highlights**. Write your own notes anywhere

block.

**Command palette → Reading mode** shows the open note as a page to read,
with the same themes, size and width. It is made for pages clipped from the
web: the source and the date the page was clipped are shown at the top.

highlight lives in the Markdown and syncs with it. A passage across

pages.title: Export and import
pages.description: Take the whole vault out as a .zip or a folder, bring in an Obsidian vault or a Notion export, and convert single files to and from many formats.
pages.md:
Your notes are plain Markdown, and they can always leave Lumen.

## The whole vault

**Export:** `⌘K → Export the whole vault…`. Pick a **.zip** download or,
where the browser can write folders (Chrome, Edge), a **folder**. Every note
and attachment is written with its folder path. A folder export goes into
a new `lumen-vault-<date>` subfolder, so nothing already in the folder you
picked is overwritten. The note you are editing is saved first.

**Import:** `⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`.
Pick a .zip or a folder. Lumen recognises:

| Source | Recognised by | What import does |
|---|---|---|
| Obsidian vault | an `.obsidian/` folder | notes and attachments as they are; `.obsidian/` itself is skipped |
| Notion export | most file names end in Notion's 32-character ID | IDs are removed from the names, and the links between pages are rewritten to the new names |
| Lumen export, or any folder | otherwise | everything as it is |

Everything is imported into a **new folder** (`Imported/<name>`, numbered
when that name is taken), so no existing note is ever overwritten. Two
pages that end up with the same name are numbered (`Page 2.md`).
`.git`, `.trash`, `__MACOSX` and `.DS_Store` are skipped. When the import
finishes, a message says how many notes and files came in and where.

## One document

**Out:** the *File* menu and the palette export the open note to HTML,
Word (.doc), RTF, LaTeX, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc, Org-mode, OPML,
slides (Reveal.js), EPUB, Jupyter (.ipynb), PowerPoint (.pptx), a static
site, and PDF (`⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`). Right-to-left text keeps its
direction in the exported files.

**In:** open a file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window. Besides Markdown and
text, Lumen converts HTML, RTF, CSV / TSV, JSON, XML, Word (.docx and the
older .doc), OpenDocument (.odt), PowerPoint (.pptx), Excel (.xlsx),
EPUB, PDF (with OCR for scanned pages), MHTML, OPML, LaTeX,
reStructuredText, AsciiDoc, Org-mode, Jupyter notebooks, Apple Pages /
Numbers / Keynote, Fountain screenplays and .zip archives into a Markdown
note.

## How it is tested

The vault round trip (export, then import), the Obsidian and Notion
detection, Notion's link rewrite and the duplicate-name numbering are unit
tests over `src/storage/exportAll.ts`. Each format converter has its own
tests.

A real corpus (`src/__tests__/fixtures/real-corpus`, with a manifest of
each file's source, licence and sha256) checks the importers end to end: 30
Word files written by LibreOffice, 30 Notion exports (Markdown & CSV, and
HTML) and 35 real Evernote exports. Each note must keep its headings,
nested lists, tables, links, images and right-to-left text. Word imports
bring numbered and nested lists, links, Hebrew bold and italic, and images
(inline, up to 512 KB each).

pages.title: Graph and local graph
pages.description: The knowledge graph of the whole vault — 10,000 notes and 50,000 links — and the local graph of the open note, with filters, colour groups and full keyboard use.
pages.md:
## The graph

**Knowledge Graph** (command palette) shows every note of the vault, and a line
for every `[[link]]` between two notes.

- **Big vaults.** The graph is built from the vault index, so the notes
  are not read again. The layout is computed in a background worker; the
  picture appears at once and settles over a second or two. Nodes and
  links are drawn with WebGL, so 10,000 notes and 50,000 links pan and
  zoom smoothly. While you move the view, a sample of the links is drawn;
  all of them come back as soon as you stop.
- **Filters.** Narrow the graph by **tag** (nested tags included:
  `project` keeps `project/active`), by **folder** (and its subfolders),
  or by a frontmatter **property**: `status=open`, or just `status` for any
  note that has one.
- **Colour groups.** Colour the notes by their top folder or their first
  tag. The legend shows the twelve biggest groups.
- **Labels** show for the bigger notes, and for more of them as you zoom
  in. Hebrew names are shaped and written right to left.

## The local graph

**Show / hide the local graph** opens a panel beside the note: the open
note in the middle, and the notes within **1, 2 or 3** links of it. It has
the same tag and folder filters, and is coloured by folder. It follows you
as you open other notes, and opens in well under a fifth of a second.

## With the keyboard

The graph is one focusable area. Tab to it, and:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| ← ↑ → ↓ | go to the linked note in that direction (or, if there is none, the nearest note that way) |
| Enter | open the focused note |
| + / − | zoom in / out |
| 0 | fit the whole graph |
| Shift + arrows | pan |
| Home | back to the biggest note (in the local graph: the open note) |

The focused note's name and number of links are announced to screen
readers. In the full graph, the **Find a note** box jumps to any note by
name, so every note can be reached without a mouse.

pages.title: Daily notes and the Hebrew calendar
pages.description: The calendar's holidays, fasts and weekly Torah portion, for Israel or the diaspora, and the {{holiday}} and {{parasha}} placeholders of the daily note.
pages.md:
**Show / hide the calendar** (command palette) shows a month under the file tree. A day with a daily
note is marked; clicking a day opens its note, or creates it from your
template.

## Holidays and the Torah portion

The calendar knows the Jewish year: the festivals, the fasts, Rosh Chodesh,
the Israeli national days, and the Torah portion of every Shabbat.

- Days with a holiday or a fast have a mark on top. Hover a day, or reach
  it with a screen reader, for its civil date, its Hebrew date, its holidays
  and, on Shabbat, its portion.
- Under the grid, the month's holidays are listed by day.
- Names are in Hebrew when the UI is in Hebrew, and in English otherwise.

### Israel or the diaspora

The festivals have one day of yom tov in Israel and two in the diaspora, so
the two calendars differ: Simchat Torah, the eighth day of Pesach and the
second day of Shavuot are diaspora days only. When one of them falls on
Shabbat, Israel reads the next Torah portion that week, and the two
schedules realign a few weeks later, when the diaspora reads two portions
together and Israel reads them separately.

The **⚙ settings** of the calendar have a checkbox,
**Holidays and Torah portions as in Israel**. Until you change it, Lumen
picks Israel when the UI is in Hebrew or your time zone is Israel's.

### What is included

| | |
|---|---|
| Festivals | Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Sukkot with Chol HaMoed and Hoshana Raba, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah, Pesach with Chol HaMoed, Shavuot |
| Fasts | Tzom Gedaliah, 10 Tevet, Ta'anit Esther, Ta'anit Bechorot, 17 Tammuz, Tish'a B'Av |
| Other days | Chanukah, Tu BiShvat, Purim Katan, Purim, Shushan Purim, Pesach Sheni, Lag BaOmer, Tu B'Av, the eve of the festivals, Rosh Chodesh |
| Israeli days | Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron, Yom HaAtzmaut, Yom Yerushalayim |

Fasts that fall on Shabbat move as they do in practice: Tzom Gedaliah,
17 Tammuz and Tish'a B'Av to Sunday, Ta'anit Esther and Ta'anit Bechorot to
Thursday. Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron and Yom HaAtzmaut move as Israeli law
sets them, so that they never touch Shabbat.

## In the daily note

Two placeholders join `{{date}}`, `{{hebrewDate}}`, `{{weekday}}` and
`{{title}}` in the daily-note template:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{{holiday}}` | the day's holidays, separated by `·`, or nothing |
| `{{parasha}}` | this week's Torah portion (the Shabbat on or after the day), or the festival read instead |

For example, the template

```markdown
# {{title}}

{{hebrewDate}} · {{parasha}} {{holiday}}
```

gives, on Friday 16 May 2025 in Israel, a line with the Hebrew date,
`Emor` and `Lag BaOmer` (in a Hebrew UI: `פרשת אמור` and `ל״ג בעומר`).

## How it is computed

The calendar is Lumen's own code: the fixed Hebrew calendar (the molad and
the four postponements of Rosh Hashana), the holiday rules, and the rules
for which Torah portions are read together, from the Shulchan Aruch. No
calendar library is used; the common one is under the GPL, which Lumen
does not ship. A whole year — holidays and every Shabbat, for Israel and
for the diaspora — is computed in a few milliseconds, in your browser.

The tests check the arithmetic against the browser's own Hebrew calendar on
every day from 1990 to 2060, and every holiday rule against a hand-checked
table of the years 2025–2030.


## Your morning

`⌘K` → **Daily note: “Your morning”** adds a block to today's note, and from
then on writes it each morning when you open today's note. It is off until
you run it, and `⌘K` → **Daily note: turn off “Your morning”** stops it.

The block has:

- the Hebrew date, this week's parasha and today's holidays;
- the notes changed since the last morning, newest first (daily notes are
  left out);
- the open tasks due today or earlier. Due dates can be written as
  `📅 2026-11-12` (Tasks), `[due:: 2026-11-12]` (Dataview) or
  `@due(2026-11-12)`;
- how many review cards are waiting, with the first few.

Every row links to its note or card.

Everything comes from this device: the vault index that search keeps in
memory, `.lumen/review.json` and the Hebrew calendar. Nothing is sent
anywhere. On a 10,000-note vault the block takes a few milliseconds, once
the index is built.

The block sits between `<!-- lumen:morning:start -->` and
`<!-- lumen:morning:end -->`. Writing it again replaces only that part, so
your own text in the note stays as it is. While today's note is open with
edits, the block is written into the editor instead of the file.

pages.title: Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero)
pages.description: Bring your highlights from Kindle, Kobo, Readwise and Zotero into the vault, one note per book, with no duplicates when you import again.
pages.md:
Run `⌘K → "Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero)…"`, pick
where the highlights come from, then pick the file.

| From | What to pick |
|---|---|
| **Kindle** | `My Clippings.txt` in the Kindle's `documents` folder (connect it by USB). |
| **Kobo** | `KoboReader.sqlite` in the reader's hidden `.kobo` folder. |
| **Readwise** | The CSV export: Readwise → Export → CSV. |
| **Zotero** | Nothing to pick: Zotero 7 on this computer, desktop app only (see below). |

Every book or article gets a note, `Highlights/ — .md`. Each
highlight is a quote with:

- its place (page, location, or chapter and %);
- the date;
- tags and your note;
- for Zotero, a link that opens the annotation in its PDF.

Hebrew titles and texts work, file names included.

## Import again, any time

Importing the same file again only adds what's new:

- A highlight that's already in the note is left as it is, including any
  edits you made to it.
- If the app changed it (for example, you edited its note in Readwise),
  the entry is updated.
- A highlight you extended on the Kindle replaces the shorter one.
- The same passage from two apps (a Kindle highlight that Readwise also
  has) is **one** entry.
- Whatever you write in the note outside the highlights is kept.

Bookmarks, Kobo dog-ears and Zotero image or ink annotations have no text
and are left out; the import says how many.

Imported highlights appear in [All highlights](/workspace/highlights/)
under the kind **Imported**, and can be searched like the rest.

## Zotero

Zotero 7 serves your library to other apps on the same computer.

1. Turn it on in Zotero: **Settings → Advanced → "Allow other applications
   on this computer to communicate with Zotero"**.
2. With Zotero open, run the import in the **desktop app**. It reads your
   annotations from `127.0.0.1` (your own computer) and never from the
   cloud.

Zotero refuses requests from web pages, so in the browser the import
explains this instead.

Nothing is uploaded: the files are read on this device, and the only
request made is the desktop app's request to Zotero on this computer.

pages.description: Every highlight from PDFs, books and clipped pages in one place: search them, tag them, export them to a note with links back, or drag one into a note.
pages.md:
**Command palette → All highlights** lists every highlight in your vault:

- from **PDFs**, kept in `file.pdf.md` ([PDF reader](/workspace/pdf-reader/)),
- from **EPUB books**, kept in `book.epub.md` ([EPUB reader](/workspace/epub-reader/)),
- from **clipped pages**: passages marked `==like this==` in a note that was
  clipped from the web, or marked in [reading mode](/workspace/epub-reader/#reading-mode-for-clipped-pages).

## Find

Type in the search box to search the highlighted text, its note and its tags.
Case, spacing and Hebrew niqqud don't matter. Narrow the list by **kind**
(PDF, EPUB, clips), by **document** and by **tag**. Click a highlight to
open it: the reader opens at its page or chapter and flashes it.

## Tags

pages.title: Import from other apps
pages.description: Bring notes from Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Apple Notes, Google Keep, Logseq or OneNote — into a new folder, with a report, undone in one click.
pages.md:
**File → Import notes from another app…** (or the command palette) opens
the import wizard. It never touches what you already have: everything goes
into a new folder, `Imported/<name of the export>`, numbered when the name
is taken. One click — **Undo the import** in the wizard, or the command
**Undo the last import** later — takes it back.

## Three steps

1. **Pick the app** the notes come from. The wizard tells you how to export
   from it.
2. **Pick the export** — a file, several files, or a folder (or drop them on
   the wizard). Archives are opened, also archives inside archives (Notion
   zips its parts). If the files look like another app's export, the wizard
   says so and switches in one click.
3. **Check, then import.** Before anything is written you see how many
   notes, attachments and databases will come in, what will not and why,
   and how many internal links reach their note.

## What each app becomes

| App | Export to pick | What it becomes |
|---|---|---|
| Obsidian | the vault folder, or a .zip of it | the vault as it is; `.obsidian/` and `.trash/` are left out |
| Notion | Settings → Export → *Markdown & CSV* or *HTML*, the .zip as it came | names without Notion's ids; links follow the pages; **each database becomes a `.base` file** with the same columns, and each row a note whose properties are the row's cells (Yes/No, numbers and dates typed) |
| Evernote | `.enex` files (one per notebook) | a folder per notebook; tasks, images and files in place (`_resources/<note>/`); tags, author, source URL, created and updated as properties; links between notes as `[[wikilinks]]`; encrypted parts are left out and reported |
| Bear | a backup (`.bearbk`) or TextBundles | a note per bundle with its `assets/`; `::highlight::` → `==highlight==`, `#multi word tag#` → `#multi-word-tag`; trashed notes left out |
| Apple Notes | HTML or Markdown from an exporter app | a note per page; images inside the HTML (`data:` URIs) become files; links between pages follow |
| Google Keep | Google Takeout (Keep only), the .zip | checklists as tasks; labels as tags; colour and pin as properties; archived notes in `Archive/`; trashed notes left out |
| Logseq | the graph folder, or a .zip | page properties as frontmatter; `TODO`/`DONE` as tasks; block references `((id))` and `{{embed}}` as `[[Page#^id]]` / `![[…]]`; journals named by date (`2024-01-31`); `a___b` pages as folders |
| OneNote | pages or sections saved as *Single File Web Page* (`.mht`) | a note per page, its images and attached files next to it |

Dates are kept as the properties `created` and `updated` (a browser cannot
set a file's own dates). Hebrew names — files, folders, tags, properties —
stay as they are; only characters a file system refuses are replaced.

## The report

The last step shows what came in, what did not and why (the app's own
settings, its trash, a second copy of a file, a format the app cannot
convert, a damaged file), notes that came with something missing (an
attachment the export does not have, an encrypted part, no dates), and links
that point at nothing. **Save the report as a note** puts it in the import's
folder (undo takes it back too).

## Undo

Undo deletes exactly what the import wrote: its folder, and `Imported/` when
the import made it. The vault is then the same, byte for byte, as before the
import. If you changed something in the folder after the import, undo moves
the folder to the trash instead, so nothing of yours is lost.

## Limits

- Apple Notes has no export of its own, and reading its database needs the
  Mac app; the wizard imports what an exporter app saved.
- OneNote's own `.one` files cannot be read; export pages or sections as
  `.mht`.
- Notion's links to a block (`#…` after a page) go to the page: the block
  ids do not survive the export.

## How it is checked

`src/__tests__/importWizard.test.ts` imports one golden export per app
(`src/__tests__/fixtures/import/exports.ts`): 0 attachments lost, at least
98 % of internal links resolved, the Notion database as a `.base` with the
same columns and rows, and an undo that gives back the same vault hash.
`e2e/import-wizard.spec.ts` runs the wizard in the browser. The golden
exports are written from each app's documented format; real exports from
the apps are the owner's check.

pages.title: Israeli time
pages.description: A Sunday–Thursday work week, the Hebrew date next to dates, and deadlines that move off Shabbat and chagim with a note saying why.
pages.md:
Lumen's calendar knows the Israeli week and the Jewish holidays (from its own
[Hebrew calendar](/workspace/hebrew-calendar/)). Nothing here rewrites a note: a moved
deadline is a suggestion shown next to the date you wrote.

## Settings

Open the calendar under the file tree and click its settings button.

| Setting | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| Work week | Sunday–Thursday when holidays are as in Israel, else Monday–Friday | In a Sunday–Thursday week Friday and Shabbat are the weekend; in a Monday–Friday week, Shabbat and Sunday. The calendar draws days off in a muted colour. |
| Hebrew dates | On for a Hebrew interface | The Hebrew date next to dates in a note's properties and in database views: `א׳ בתשרי תשפ״ז` in Hebrew, `1 Tishri 5787` otherwise. |
| A deadline on Shabbat or a chag | Suggest the next working day | Or the previous working day, or don't move it (only say why). |

The calendar starts the week on Sunday for Hebrew (and English), and on Monday for
French, German and Russian, as each language's own calendar does.

## Which days are off

- **Shabbat**, and the weekend of your work week.
- **Every yom tov:** Rosh Hashana (two days), Yom Kippur, the first day of Sukkot, Shemini
  Atzeret, the first and seventh days of Pesach and Shavuot. In the diaspora, the second
  days too. These are the Jewish rest days of the Hours of Work and Rest Law, 1951 (§18A).
- **Yom HaAtzmaut**, in Israel: a statutory holiday (Independence Day Law, 1949), on the
  day the government rules set (moved off Friday, Shabbat and Monday).

These days are working days, but get a note: **erev chag** (often a short day),
**Chol HaMoed** (many offices close), **fasts** (Tzom Gedaliah, 17 Tammuz, Tisha B'Av…),
**Yom HaZikaron** and **Yom HaShoah**.

## Deadlines

A **deadline** is a property named `due`, `deadline`, `due_date`, `יעד`, `תאריך יעד`,
`דדליין` or `מועד אחרון`. If it falls on a day off, you get a note:

> due: 2026-09-12 (א׳ בתשרי תשפ״ז) ⚠ Falls on Shabbat · Rosh Hashana I: suggested 2026-09-14 (Tzom Gedaliah)

Moving to the **next** working day is how Israeli law counts a period whose last day is a
day of rest (Interpretation Law, 1981, §10). Choose **previous** if you'd rather finish
before the chag.

### In a database view

Name the deadline column in the `database` block:

````md
```database
source: projects/
view: table
fields: [status, due]
deadline: due        # moved off Shabbat / chag, working days left
hebrewDate: true     # optional: overrides the setting for this block
```
````

The deadline column shows the date, the Hebrew date, the suggested working day when it
moves, and **working days left** (or overdue), counted over your work week and the
holidays. In the **calendar** view, every day has its Hebrew date and holidays, and each
item whose deadline is a day off has the suggestion under it.

## Checked

`src/__tests__/israeliTime.test.ts` has 30 golden deadlines from 2026 to 2028: every chag
on a weekday and on Shabbat, erev chag, Chol HaMoed, Yom HaAtzmaut's moves, the previous
working day, the diaspora's second days and a Monday–Friday week. Each Hebrew date is
checked against the browser's own Hebrew calendar (ICU) as well as Lumen's.

pages.title: Jewish sources from Sefaria
pages.description: Quote a verse, a mishnah or a Talmud folio by its reference, with each text's licence. Keep a copy for offline use, and see every note that cites the same verse.
pages.md:
Type a reference the way you write it, such as `בראשית א:א`, `ב״ר א, א`,
`שמות כ׳ ג׳`, `Gen. 1:1-3` or `ברכות ב.`. Lumen brings the text from
[Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org), the open library of Jewish texts, with
its niqqud and cantillation as they are.

## Quote a source

1. Select the reference in the source editor, or put the cursor on its line.
2. Open the command palette (⌘K) and run **Insert a source from Sefaria…**.
   With nothing selected, Lumen asks for the reference.
3. **Confirm the lookup.** The question says exactly what is sent: only the
   reference (for example `Genesis 1:1`), nothing from your notes.

The quote replaces the reference:

```markdown
> **[[Genesis.1.1|בראשית א׳:א׳]]**
>
> בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים …
>
> — [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1) · עברית: Miqra according to the Masorah ([CC-BY-SA](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)) · English: … (CC-BY-NC) — link only
```

Every version's title and licence are written next to it. The link
`[[Genesis.1.1|…]]` makes the verse a node in the graph.

## Licences: what is copied and what is only linked

Sefaria gives each version of a text, in each language, its own licence.
Lumen reads that licence from Sefaria's own data and follows it:

| Licence | In your note | In the offline copy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public Domain, CC0 | the text | the text |
| CC-BY, CC-BY-SA | the text, with its credit and licence | the text, with its credit and licence |
| CC-BY-NC, CC-BY-NC-SA, CC-BY-NC-ND | a link only | not stored |
| Copyright, or no licence noted | a link only | not stored |

**Non-commercial licences count as not free.** A note travels: it syncs,
gets published and gets exported, and Lumen cannot know what it will be used
for. **"No licence noted" means Sefaria has not checked the copyright yet.**
A non-free text is dropped as soon as Sefaria's answer is read. It never
reaches a note, the vault or a cache.

## Keep a copy for offline use

Saving is your choice and never automatic. Use the **Save for offline**
button on the message after a quote, or run **Save this source for offline**.
The copy goes to `Sources/Sefaria/.md`:

- **its frontmatter** records every version's title, licence, licence link and
  source, and whether it was copied;
- **its body** holds the free texts only.

Once a source is saved, quoting it again uses the copy: no request, no
question, and it works with no network at all.

## My notes on this verse

Put the cursor on a reference, or open a saved source note, and run **My notes
on this verse**. Lumen lists every note that cites the verse, through a wiki
link (`[[בראשית א:א]]`, `[[Genesis.1.1]]`) or a Sefaria link. The search
reads your vault on this device and sends nothing.

## Privacy

A lookup sends only the reference to `www.sefaria.org`. The privacy ledger
lists each lookup as a consented request, and the cloud-routes table lists it
as `sefaria-texts`. The *local only* policy doesn't block a lookup you
confirmed, the same way it treats a diagram you chose to send.

## What is recognised

- **Books:**
  - the Tanakh, with Hebrew and English names and the usual abbreviations
    (`בר׳`, `ש״א`, `Gen.`, `1 Sam`);
  - Midrash Rabbah (`ב״ר`, `שמו״ר` …);
  - the Mishnah (`משנה ברכות א:א`, `אבות א:א`);
  - the Babylonian Talmud (`ברכות ב.`, `ב״מ נט:`, `Berakhot 2a`).
- **Numbers** can be Hebrew numerals, with or without geresh or gershayim
  (`קי״ט`, `טו`), or digits. A range is written `א:א-ג`.
- **Not supported yet:** commentaries (`רש״י על בראשית א:א`), the Jerusalem
  Talmud, halakhic codes, and ranges that cross chapters.

## About Sefaria

Lumen uses Sefaria's public texts API, which needs no key. "Sefaria" is a
trademark of Sefaria; Lumen is not made or endorsed by Sefaria.

pages.title: JSON Canvas (Obsidian .canvas)
pages.description: Open Obsidian canvases in Lumen's Excalidraw canvas and write them back as .canvas files. JSON Canvas is an open, MIT-licensed format.
pages.md:
[JSON Canvas](https://jsoncanvas.org) is the open format Obsidian uses for its
canvases (`.canvas` files, spec 1.0, MIT licensed). Lumen's
[canvas](/workspace/canvas/) reads and writes it. Everything runs on your device.

## Import

- **Import .canvas** in the canvas bar: pick a `.canvas` file. It becomes a new
  canvas, `canvases/<name>.excalidraw`, and opens. If that name is taken, you
  get `<name>-2`, `<name>-3` and so on, and nothing is overwritten.
- A `.canvas` file already in the vault's `canvases/` folder (for example from
  a synced Obsidian vault) is listed in the picker with a **Convert** button,
  like old tldraw canvases. The `.canvas` file stays as it was.

## Export

**Export .canvas** writes the open canvas to `canvases/<name>.canvas`, next to
its `.excalidraw` file, byte for byte in Obsidian's own layout (tabs, one
node or edge per line, no space after a colon). A canvas from Obsidian that
you import and export without edits comes back byte-identical.
Exporting again replaces that `.canvas` file. The `.excalidraw` file is not
touched.

## How it maps

| JSON Canvas | Excalidraw |
|---|---|
| Text node (Markdown) | Rectangle with the text inside (shown as written, not rendered) |
| File node (`file`, `subpath`) | Rectangle showing the path, with the path as the element's link |
| Link node (`url`) | Rectangle showing the URL, with the URL as the element's link |
| Group (`label`) | Frame with the label as its name. Nodes inside it belong to the frame (to the smallest one, since Excalidraw frames don't nest) |
| Edge (`fromSide`/`toSide`, `fromEnd`/`toEnd`, `label`) | Arrow bound to both nodes at those sides, with arrowheads per end and the label on the arrow |
| Colour: preset `1`–`6` or hex | Stroke colour (the presets as Obsidian draws them: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, purple) |

**Round trip.** Each element keeps the node or edge it came from, so a canvas
that is imported and exported without edits comes back the same, including
what Excalidraw has no place for: a file's subpath, a group's background, and
fields added by other apps. Edits are written back. Moved or resized nodes,
changed text, a changed link (`Notes/Plan.md#Goals` → `file` + `subpath`),
recoloured elements and arrows that now connect different nodes are all
exported.

**Drawn in Excalidraw.** Rectangles, ellipses and diamonds become text nodes
(with the text inside them), a shape with a link becomes a link or file node,
free text becomes a text node, frames become groups, and arrows bound to two
of those become edges. Images, free-hand strokes, lines and arrows not
connected at both ends have no JSON Canvas form. They are left out of the
`.canvas` file, the export says how many, and they stay in the
`.excalidraw` canvas.

sections.heading: JSON Canvas (Obsidian .canvas)
sections.text: JSON Canvas is the open format Obsidian uses for its canvases (.canvas files, spec 1.0, MIT licensed). Lumen's canvas reads and writes it. Everything runs on your device.

sections.heading: Import
sections.text: Import .canvas in the canvas bar: pick a .canvas file. It becomes a new canvas, canvases/ .excalidraw, and opens. If that name is taken, you get -2, -3 and so on, and nothing is overwritten. A .canvas file already in the vault's canvases/ folder (for example from a synced Obsidian vault) is listed in the picker with a Convert button, like old tldraw canvases. The .canvas file stays as it was.

sections.heading: Export
sections.text: Export .canvas writes the open canvas to canvases/ .canvas, next to its .excalidraw file, byte for byte in Obsidian's own layout (tabs, one node or edge per line, no space after a colon). A canvas from Obsidian that you import and export without edits comes back byte-identical. Exporting again replaces that .canvas file. The .excalidraw file is not touched.

sections.heading: How it maps
sections.text: JSON Canvas Excalidraw --- --- Text node (Markdown) Rectangle with the text inside (shown as written, not rendered) File node (file, subpath) Rectangle showing the path, with the path as the element's link Link node (url) Rectangle showing the URL, with the URL as the element's link Group (label) Frame with the label as its name. Nodes inside it belong to the frame (to the smallest one, since Excalidraw frames don't nest) Edge (fromSide/toSide, fromEnd/toEnd, label) Arrow bound to both nodes at those sides, with arrowheads per end and the label on the arrow Colour: preset 1–6 or hex Stroke colour (the presets as Obsidian draws them: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, purple) Round trip. Each element keeps the node or edge it came from, so a canvas that is imported and exported without edits comes back the same, including what Excalidraw has no place for: a file's subpath, a group's background, and fields added by other apps. Edits are written back. Moved or resized nodes, changed text, a changed link (Notes/Plan.md#Goals → file + subpath), recoloured elements and arrows that now connect different nodes are all exported. Drawn in Excalidraw. Rectangles, ellipses and diamonds become text nodes (with the text inside them), a shape with a link becomes a link or file node, free text becomes a text node, frames become groups, and arrows bound to two of those become edges. Images, free-hand strokes, lines and arrows not connected at both ends have no JSON Canvas form. They are left out of the .canvas file, the export says how many, and they stay in the .excalidraw canvas.

pages.title: Large vaults and long notes
pages.description: How Lumen stays fast with 10,000 notes and with a single 2 MB note — and how that is measured.
pages.md:
Lumen is built to stay responsive with a vault of **10,000 notes** and with a
single note of **2 MB** (plan 8.4). Nothing needs to be switched on; this page
explains what happens and what to expect.

## A vault with thousands of notes

- **The index lives in a Web Worker.** Search (`⇧⌘F`), backlinks and the tags
  panel read one shared index of your notes. It is built once, in a
  background worker, so a query over 10,000 notes never blocks typing.
  Hebrew search (niqqud, final letters and prefix letters folded) is prepared
  when a note is indexed, not on every query.
- **A save re-indexes only that note.** After the first build, saving a note
  re-reads that note alone; renaming or deleting a note or a folder moves or
  drops its entries without reading anything. When files change behind
  Lumen's back (another tab, a folder edited elsewhere), the index re-lists
  the vault and re-reads only the files whose modification time changed.
- **The file tree and the index share one listing** of the vault after a
  structural change.
- **Big vaults open with folders collapsed.** With more than 1,000 notes the
  file tree starts with its folders closed (the folders of the open note stay
  open), so opening the vault does not render 10,000 rows.

## A very long note

From 50,000 characters on, three things change — the result on screen is the
same:

- **The outline** re-parses only the blocks that changed (a paragraph, a list,
  a code block). Opening or closing a code fence, or changing a reference
  definition (`[label]: url`), re-parses what it affects.
- **The preview** is rendered block by block. After an edit only the changed
  blocks are rendered again, and rendering pauses every few milliseconds so
  the editor stays fluid. A note with footnotes, reference definitions or
  suggestions (CriticMarkup) is rendered in one pass, as before.
- **The word count** in the status bar, and keeping a copy of the open note
  in the browser's storage for the next session, happen when you pause
  typing rather than on every keystroke.

## Targets and how they are checked

| What | Target | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open the app with 10,000 notes | < 1 s | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts` (production build) |
| Save → index updated | < 50 ms | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts`, `src/__tests__/vaultWorker.test.ts` |
| Search 10,000 notes | < 100 ms | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts`, `src/__tests__/vaultWorker.test.ts` |
| Typing in a 2 MB note | < 16 ms per keystroke | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts` (`@nightly`) |

The unit tests count work rather than time it: a save reads one note and
re-indexes one note, a rename reads none, backlinks read only the linking
notes, a keystroke in a long note re-parses one block. The outline is
compared with the one-pass outline on random documents and random edits.

The 2 MB typing test runs every night (`.github/workflows/nightly-perf.yml`),
not on every pull request. To run it yourself against a production build:

```sh
npm run build
npx http-server dist -p 5180 -c-1 --cors &
PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5180 npx playwright test --project=perf
```

Each run attaches the measured numbers to the Playwright report as `perf`
annotations.

## Responsiveness budget

Load time is measured by Lighthouse; how fast each action answers is
measured separately (plan W1.22), in Chromium with the CPU slowed 4×, like a
mid-range phone:

| What | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| INP over 20 fixed interactions (palette, view modes, opening and switching notes, typing, a task checkbox, search, undo) | p75 < 100 ms |
| Key press → next frame, end of a 50 KB note | p95 < 16 ms |
| Key press → next frame, end of a 2 MB note | p95 < 33 ms |

```sh
npm run perf:inp          # measures (e2e/inp-budget.spec.ts), then gates
npm run perf:inp:gate -- --record   # also appends the run to reports/perf/inp-trend.jsonl
```

The run writes `reports/perf/inp-latest.json`. The gate compares it with
`reports/perf/inp-baseline.json` and fails when any of the three numbers is
10 % or more slower; the first run becomes the baseline
(`npm run perf:inp:gate -- --update` replaces it on purpose).

## Responsiveness on real devices

`npm run perf:responsiveness` measures both editors (source and WYSIWYG) on
a 10,000-note vault, against the production build (plan W6.45):

| Environment | Where | INP p75 budget |
|---|---|---|
| `desktop-chromium` | Desktop Chrome, CPU as is | < 100 ms |
| `mid-phone-emulated` | Pixel 7 emulation, CPU 4× slower | < 200 ms |
| `real-device-*` | real Pixel and iPhone on BrowserStack (`perf:responsiveness -- browserstack`) | < 200 ms |

Keypress → paint p95 must stay under 16 ms in a 50 KB note and under 33 ms
in a 2 MB note, everywhere. Safari has no Event Timing API, so on an iPhone
only keypress → paint is measured; INP shows as "not measured" there,
never as 0.

The related-notes panel is open during the whole measurement, because it
re-ranks after every pause in typing. A build without the panel still runs,
but its run says `relatedPanel: false`, it scores no board number, and it is
never compared with a baseline taken with the panel. To make a new baseline,
run `node scripts/perf/responsiveness.mjs gate --update`.

Each environment has its own baseline in `reports/perf/baselines/<env>.json`.
The first run writes it; commit it. A later run fails when any number is
10 % or more slower than that baseline. The run also writes a signed
`lumen-metric` receipt to `reports/metrics/`, which the area board scores
(`perf.inp-p75-ms`, `perf.inp-p75-mid-phone-ms`, `perf.key2paint-p95-*`).
The nightly perf run and the verification factory run it every night.

## For developers

- `src/storage/vaultIndexCore.ts` — the index (pure, runs in the worker or in
  the page); `src/storage/vaultIndex.worker.ts` and
  `src/storage/vaultIndexProtocol.ts` — the worker and its messages;
  `src/storage/workspaceIndex.ts` — the main-thread side, fed by the
  VaultBackend's events (`watchVault`).
- `src/renderer/blocks.ts` — top-level blocks of a document, re-scanned only
  around an edit; `src/renderer/incrementalToc.ts` and
  `src/renderer/incrementalPreview.ts` build on it.
- Semantic-search vectors are kept as one `Float32Array` per note, with the
  norms precomputed (`packVectors` in `src/ai/semanticSearch.ts`).
