pages.title: Academic LaTeX export (Hebrew)
pages.description: Export a note as a LaTeX project — Hebrew right to left with babel, math, Pandoc-style [@key] citations from the vault's BibTeX, and images — that compiles with LuaLaTeX or XeLaTeX.
pages.md:
**Export LaTeX project (academic, Hebrew)…** in the command palette
downloads `<note>-latex.zip` with:

- `main.tex` — the note as an `article`: `#` becomes the title (or
  `title:` from the frontmatter), `##` sections, lists, quotes, tables,
  footnotes, code (left to right, verbatim), inline `$…$` and display
  `$$…$$` math as written;
- the reference list, in APA (the same formatter as Lumen's citations),
  each entry in its own language and direction;
- `references.bib` — the cited entries from every `.bib` in the vault, for
  a bibtex or biblatex style of your own;
- `images/` — the images the note shows;
- `README.txt` with the compile command.

Compile with `latexmk -lualatex main.tex` (recommended) or
`latexmk -xelatex main.tex`. Both work from the same preamble.

## Hebrew

The preamble uses **babel** with `\babelprovide[import, main]{hebrew}`
— `bidi=basic` under LuaLaTeX, which babel's maintainers recommend for
right-to-left text, and `bidi=default` under XeLaTeX. Polyglossia was not
chosen: under XeLaTeX it needs the separate `bidi` package, and babel
covers both engines with one preamble.

In a Hebrew paper every run of Latin text (a term, a name, `1–20` page
ranges, an e-mail) is wrapped in `\foreignlanguage{english}{…}`, so it
reads left to right with the right font and hyphenation; in an English
paper Hebrew runs get `\foreignlanguage{hebrew}{…}`. Math and code are
always left to right. The paper's language is decided by its letters.

Fonts: Frank Ruhl Libre or David Libre (SIL Open Font Licence, free from
Google Fonts) when installed, else Noto Serif Hebrew or FreeSerif; Latin
Modern for English.

## Citations

Pandoc's syntax, as in Lumen's citation dialog:

| In the note | In main.tex |
|---|---|
| `[@cohen2020]` | `\citep{cohen2020}` |
| `[see @knuth1984, p. 33]` | `\citep[see][p.~33]{knuth1984}` |
| `[@a; @b]` | `\citep{a,b}` |
| `@cohen2020 showed` | `\citet{cohen2020} showed` |

Only keys found in a `.bib` in the vault become citations (so an e-mail
address stays text); the toast lists cited keys that are missing.

## How it was checked

`src/__tests__/latexAcademic.test.ts` turns ten golden notes in
`src/__tests__/fixtures/latex/` (Hebrew, English, mixed runs, inline and
display math, citations, lists and quotes, a table, footnotes and links,
code and special characters, an English paper with Hebrew) into exactly the
`.tex` beside each. All ten compiled with XeLaTeX (TeX Live 2023) with no
errors and no missing characters; the PDFs read right to left.

pages.title: Literature review matrix
pages.description: One table of every PDF in the vault, with question, method, sample, findings and limitations, and each value backed by a quote verified on its page. Runs on this device.
pages.md:
`⌘K` → **Literature review from the vault's PDFs** reads every PDF in the
vault on this device. Scanned pages are read with OCR. It writes:

- **one note per paper** in `Literature review/`, with five fields as
  properties: question, method, sample, findings and limitations. Under each
  value are the quotes it came from, each with a link to its page and line;
- **`Literature review.base`**, which shows the notes as a table, one row per
  paper and one column per field (Obsidian Bases format). It has two views:
  **All papers** and **Verified only**, which lists only the papers where
  every field is verified.

## No value without a quote

For each field, the passages that search finds go to the local model. The
model answers with quotes copied from those passages. Each quote is then
looked up in its passage and located on its page:

- A value is kept only when at least one of its quotes is found.
- Quotes that were made up, or that cite the wrong passage, are dropped. If
  none is left, the field shows "No value with a verified quote" instead of
  a guess.

The model is the local one in AI settings (Ollama or the browser model). A
cloud model is used only if your AI policy allows it.

## How it is measured

`eval/probes/lit-review.json` has five short papers (English and Hebrew).
For each field it records the right page and a phrase from it.

- `src/__tests__/litReview.test.ts` runs retrieval and verification on
  them with a stand-in model. Retrieval finds the right passage for 24 of
  the 25 fields, and every kept citation is on the right page. It also
  checks that a model that makes quotes up has nothing kept.
- `npm run eval:lit-review` runs the real model and reports the share of
  fields that are right.
- The acceptance set is 20 real papers, which the owner provides in the same
  file format. The plan's targets: 85% of fields right, every citation on the
  right page.

pages.title: Mail and Google Takeout into notes
pages.description: Import .eml and .mbox mail and a Google Takeout archive (Keep, Docs) into notes, from files only, with Hebrew mail in every old encoding.
pages.md:
**⌘K → Import mail (.eml, .mbox) or Google Takeout…** reads mail and Google
data **from files only**. No account is connected and nothing leaves this
device.

## What you can pick

| Source | File |
|---|---|
| Single messages | `.eml`, saved from any mail app |
| Mailboxes | `.mbox`: Gmail's Takeout, Thunderbird, Apple Mail |
| Google Takeout | the `takeout-….zip`, with **Mail** (an `.mbox` with Gmail labels), **Keep** and **Drive** |

When the mailbox has Gmail labels, Lumen asks which label to import, or all
of them. Each label is shown with its message count.

## What you get

Everything goes into new folders in `Imported/`, and nothing existing is
overwritten:

- **Mail**: one note per **thread**, linked by `Message-ID`, `In-Reply-To`
  and `References`. Without those headers, the subject is used, minus `Re:`,
  `Fwd:`, `השב:` and `הועבר:`. Messages run oldest first, each under the
  sender and date, with To/Cc. Attachments are copied to `attachments/`:
  pictures are shown in place, other files linked. The frontmatter holds the
  subject, participants, first and last date, and labels.
- **Google Keep**: one note per Keep note. You get the text, the checklist
  as `- [ ]` / `- [x]`, labels as tags, created and edited times, pinned and
  archived, the attachments and the links. Notes in Keep's trash are left
  out, and the report says how many.
- **Google Docs**: Takeout exports Docs as `.docx` by default, and they
  become Markdown. `.odt`, `.rtf`, `.html`, `.txt` and `.md` work too. Any
  other Drive file is copied as it is, in its folder.

The folders are marked as outside content, so AI agents treat their text as
other people's words.

## Hebrew mail in old encodings

Mail from older Israeli systems often isn't UTF-8. Lumen reads:

- **windows-1255** and **ISO-8859-8-I**: Hebrew in logical order, as typed.
- **ISO-8859-8**: in MIME this label means **visual** order. Each line is
  stored as it looks on a left-to-right screen, so the Hebrew reads
  backwards (RFC 1555 and the Hebrew-mail draft that followed it). Lumen
  turns those lines around and keeps English words, numbers and links in
  their own order. Many mail apps also put normal, logical text under this
  label. Lumen tells the two apart by the final letters (ך ם ן ף ץ): they end
  words in logical text and start them in visual text. A plain כ מ נ פ צ at
  the end of a word is another sign of visual text.
- Encoded-words in subjects and names (`=?windows-1255?B?…?=`, `?Q?`, in
  any charset), file names in the `filename*=utf-8''…` form, and raw 8-bit
  headers.

## Large mailboxes

A 5,000-message mbox is read and turned into notes in about a second (measured
in the test suite; the plan's limit is 2 minutes). The whole file is read into memory, so a Takeout mbox of several GB
is best split by label in Takeout first (one `.mbox` per label).

sections.text: Mail from older Israeli systems often isn't UTF-8. Lumen reads: windows-1255 and ISO-8859-8-I : Hebrew in logical order, as typed. ISO-8859-8 : in MIME this label means visual order. Each line is stored as it looks on a left-to-right screen, so the Hebrew reads backwards (RFC 1555 and the Hebrew-mail draft that followed it). Lumen turns those lines around and keeps English words, numbers and links in their own order. Many mail apps also put normal, logical text under this label. Lumen tells the two apart by the final letters (ך ם ן ף ץ): they end words in logical text and start them in visual text. A plain כ מ נ פ צ at the end of a word is another sign of visual text. Encoded-words in subjects and names (=?windows-1255?B?…?=, ?Q?, in any charset), file names in the filename =utf-8''… form, and raw 8-bit headers.

sections.heading: Large mailboxes
sections.text: A 5,000-message mbox is read and turned into notes in about a second (measured in the test suite; the plan's limit is 2 minutes). The whole file is read into memory, so a Takeout mbox of several GB is best split by label in Takeout first (one .mbox per label).

pages.title: The vault in a folder on your phone
pages.description: In the iOS and Android apps, keep the vault in a real folder — the Files app on iOS, a folder you pick on Android — and see edits made there.
pages.md:
In the phone app the vault starts in the app's private storage. **Command
palette → Move the vault to a folder…** puts it in a real folder on the
phone, where other apps can open and edit the notes:

| | Where the vault goes |
|---|---|
| **iOS** | The app's Documents folder. In the **Files** app it is *On My iPhone › Lumen*; other apps can open and edit the notes in place. |
| **Android** | A folder you pick in the system's folder picker (any folder on the phone or the SD card). Lumen keeps the permission across restarts. If the app was built without Lumen's folder plugin, the app's own folder on the device is used instead. |

The move copies every note, reads each copy back and compares it, and only
then switches; the app storage is kept as it was. **Open a folder as the
vault…** uses a folder that already has notes, without copying.

## Edits made in other apps

Lumen checks the folder every few seconds while it is open, and at once
when you come back to it (for example from the Files app). A changed note
updates in Lumen; if you changed the same note in Lumen at the same time,
you get the conflict dialog and nothing is lost (see *Changes made outside
Lumen*).

## When the folder is gone

On Android the permission can be taken back in the system settings, or the
folder can be deleted. Lumen then shows the vault as **disconnected** and
reads and writes nothing until you pick the folder again (**Reconnect**).

## Status

The app side is complete and tested against both phone file APIs. The
native pieces are listed in `mobile/README.md` in the repository: the
official `@capacitor/filesystem` plugin (iOS and the Android fallback) and
Lumen's small Android folder plugin; checks on real devices are still open.

pages.title: Notion's formulas in Bases
pages.description: Notion's formula functions (dates, text, numbers, lists with current and index, lookups through relations) inside .base formulas and filters, plus two for Hebrew.
pages.md:
A `.base` formula or filter can use Notion's formula functions next to
Obsidian's own, so a database brought over from Notion keeps its formulas.
Where a name is already an Obsidian function (`if`, `min`, `max`, `empty`,
`now`, `today`, `link`, `date`, `list`, `number`), Obsidian's meaning stays,
because a `.base` file must mean in Lumen what it means in Obsidian.

## The functions

| Group | Functions |
|---|---|
| Logic | `ifs`, `let`, `lets`, `equal`, `unequal`, `prop("Name")` |
| Text | `length`, `substring`, `contains`, `test`, `match`, `replace` (the first match), `replaceAll`, `lower`, `upper`, `trim`, `repeat`, `split`, `join`, `format`, `concat` |
| Numbers | `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, `mod`, `pow`, `abs`, `round(n, places)`, `ceil`, `floor`, `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `sign`, `exp`, `ln`, `log10`, `log2`, `sum`, `mean`, `median`, `toNumber`, `pi`, `e` |
| Dates | `dateAdd`, `dateSubtract`, `dateBetween`, `formatDate`, `parseDate`, `timestamp`, `fromTimestamp`, `year`, `month` (1–12), `week` (ISO), `day` (1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday), `dayOfMonth` (Notion's `date()`), `hour`, `minute` |
| Lists | `map`, `filter`, `find`, `findIndex`, `some`, `every`, `count`: the expression sees `current` and `index`. `at` (a negative index counts from the end), `first`, `last`, `slice`, `sort`, `reverse`, `unique`, `includes`, `flat` |
| Relations | `relation.<name>` (the related notes), `current.prop("X")` on one of them, `lookup(relation.<name>, "X")`, `rollup.<name>` |
| Hebrew | `hebrewDate(date)` gives "ב׳ בכסלו תשפ״ז", and `hebrewDate(date, "day" \| "month" \| "year")` one part. `stripNikud(text)` removes the vowel marks |

`dateBetween(a, b, unit)` is a − b in whole units, toward zero, as in
Notion. Units are years, quarters, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes,
seconds and milliseconds. An empty date or number gives an empty result, so
a row without the property shows nothing instead of an error.

## Examples

```yaml
relations:
  subs: { property: Parent, incoming: true }
formulas:
  daysLeft: dateBetween(Due, today(), "days")
  hours: sum(map(relation.subs, current.prop("Estimate")))
  done: round(count(relation.subs, current.prop("Done")) / length(relation.subs) * 100) + "%"
  priority: ifs(Priority == 1, "High", Priority == 2, "Medium", "Low")
  hebrew: hebrewDate(Due)
```

## For scripts and plugins

A plugin with the `bases:read` permission reads a view's rows with
`lumen.bases.query()`. With `bases:write`, `lumen.bases.update()` changes note
properties behind one approval screen per call. See
[Plugin API](/plugins/api/). Automations can run
[when a row of a base changes](/workspace/automations/).

## Speed

10,000 notes, with two filters for every view, one view filter, a formula
column and a two-key sort, run in tens of milliseconds once warm. Simple
filter statements (a property compared with a value, `file.inFolder`,
`file.hasTag`, and `&&`, `||`, `!` of those) run without the interpreter,
with the same results.

## How it was checked

A golden set of 53 formulas as Notion users write them, with the values
Notion documents (`src/__tests__/basesNotion.test.ts`), uses every function
above.
